report:
**Conclusion: No — hydroxychloroquine does not reduce the likelihood of dying from COVID-19.**

The evidence against a mortality benefit is robust and comes from multiple large randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analyses:

1. **RECOVERY Trial (NEJM, 2020):** The largest RCT of hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized COVID-19 patients (1,561 on HCQ vs. 3,155 on usual care) found no difference in 28-day mortality, duration of hospital stay, or risk of progressing to mechanical ventilation. The trial arm was halted for futility in June 2020.
   — https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926

2. **WHO Solidarity Trial (NEJM, 2020):** This multinational RCT found that hydroxychloroquine produced "little or no reduction in the mortality of hospitalized COVID-19 patients" compared to standard of care, with no benefit in any subgroup.
   — https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine

3. **Meta-analysis (Nature Communications, 2021):** A pooled analysis of multiple studies found that hydroxychloroquine was associated with *increased* mortality in COVID-19 patients, and chloroquine showed no benefit.
   — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z

4. **NIH conclusion:** The NIH formally concluded that hydroxychloroquine "provides no clinical benefit to hospitalized patients."
   — https://www.nih.gov/news-events/news-releases/hydroxychloroquine-does-not-benefit-adults-hospitalized-covid-19

**On the other side:** Early in the pandemic, small or non-randomized studies and anecdotal reports suggested possible benefit, fueling significant public interest. However, these were systematically disproven by the large RCTs above, which represent the gold standard of medical evidence.

In summary, the totality of high-quality evidence — including the two largest RCTs and multiple meta-analyses — confirms that hydroxychloroquine does not reduce COVID-19 mortality, and may even increase it due to cardiac side effects.
